clips.title: The Confused Deputy Problem
clips.why: The broker holds strong keys and acts for a weak caller, which is exactly the setting of a confused deputy.
look: The deputy has authority the caller does not have.
The harm happens when the deputy uses its own authority for the caller's request without checking it.
The fix in every example: check what the caller itself is allowed to ask for.
clips.after: Our broker is the deputy, and the scope is how it knows what the caller, one run, is allowed to ask for.

clips.title: Build an API Proxy Server - Hide Your API Keys, Rate Limiting & Caching
clips.why: A small server adds a secret key to requests on the server side, so the client never sees it; the broker does the same for GitHub, Jira and Slack.
look: The key is read from the server's environment, never sent to the client.
The client calls the proxy, and the proxy calls the real API.
What is missing for us: this proxy forwards anything. Ours checks a scope first.
clips.after: The broker is this proxy plus a scope per run: it adds the token only after the request passed the check for its own field.

practice.q: Complete the Jira comment route so it refuses every issue except the run's own.
practice.after: ? [200, { commented: s.jiraKey }] : [403, { error: `only ${s.jiraKey} can be commented on` }]
practice.hint: The scope field that holds the run's one ticket.
practice.why: Each route compares the request with its own field of the scope.

practice.q: Which status should the broker return when the capability is unknown, and which when the run is known but asks for another thread?

options.text: 401 for the unknown capability, 403 for the other thread
options.why: 401 means "I do not know who you are"; 403 means "I know you, and this is not yours".
An unknown capability is not a known caller. Keeping the two apart makes the audit lines useful.

options.text: 404 for both, to hide that the route exists
options.why: The routes are no secret. Clear refusals with reasons help Nova stop and ask.

practice.q: Put the life of a run's scope in order.
items: The orchestrator opens the scope on the internal port
The broker stores the hash of a new capability next to the scope
The orchestrator writes the capability onto the VM
Each request from the VM is checked against one field of the scope
The workflow's cleanup step deletes the scope, and every route answers 401
practice.why: One scope is opened, used at every door and closed with one call.

practice.q: Why is the route that opens a scope on an internal port, not on the port the VMs use?

options.text: So a VM can use its scope but never open or widen one
options.why: If the VM could reach that route, a fooled agent could give itself a bigger scope.

options.text: Because the internal port is faster
options.why: Speed has nothing to do with it. It is about who can reach the route.

options.text: Because the VMs have no network at all
options.why: The VMs reach the broker's sandbox port over PrivateLink. They just cannot reach the internal one.
